facts.summary: South Dakota has no state overtime or comp-time law, so federal FLSA rules (overtime after 40 hours per week) govern.
facts.citation: No state overtime statute; FLSA governs
facts.sourceAgency: South Dakota Department of Labor & Regulation
facts.notes: State page states verbatim: 'South Dakota has no labor laws concerning compensatory (comp) time or overtime.' Federal FLSA controls.

facts.summary: South Dakota's minimum wage is $11.85/hour effective January 1, 2026, higher than the federal $7.25.
facts.citation: SDCL 60-11-3 (base minimum wage provision); SDCL 60-11-3.2 (annual CPI adjustment and publication authority)
facts.sourceAgency: South Dakota Department of Labor & Regulation
facts.notes: Confirmed against both the DLR's Oct. 23, 2025 press release (rate rising from $11.50 to $11.85/hr effective Jan. 1, 2026) and the primary statute text on sdlegislature.gov. Note: SDCL 60-11-3's own codified text still states the original $8.50/hr floor set by Initiated Measure 18 (2014); the current $11.85 figure is the CPI-adjusted rate the Secretary of Labor & Regulation is required to publish annually by Oct. 15 under SDCL 60-11-3.2, not literally written into 60-11-3's codified text -- so 60-11-3.2 is now cited alongside 60-11-3 for accuracy.

facts.summary: South Dakota's tipped-employee minimum cash wage is $5.925/hour effective January 1, 2026 (half the standard minimum wage).
facts.sourceAgency: South Dakota Department of Labor & Regulation
facts.notes: Confirmed directly against the primary statute text (SDCL 60-11-3.1, 'Minimum wage for tipped employees') on sdlegislature.gov, which sets the tipped cash wage at not less than 50% of the § 60-11-3 minimum wage, and against DLR's Oct. 23, 2025 press release confirming $5.925/hr effective Jan. 1, 2026 (half of $11.85).

facts.summary: South Dakota's minimum wage is adjusted annually for cost of living using the Consumer Price Index, rounded up to the nearest 5 cents, and can never decrease.
facts.sourceAgency: South Dakota Legislative Research Council (South Dakota Codified Laws)
facts.notes: Confirmed directly against the primary statute text: SDCL 60-11-3.2 ('Annual minimum wage adjustment') requires the wage to be adjusted each January 1 by the August-over-August percentage increase in the CPI-U (or successor index), rounded up to the nearest 5 cents, with a floor of no decrease, and requires DLR to publish the adjusted rate by October 15 each year. Enacted by the same 2014 ballot measure (Initiated Measure 18) as § 60-11-3.

facts.summary: South Dakota employment discrimination law covers race, color, creed, religion, sex, national origin, ancestry, and disability, adding creed and ancestry beyond the federal Title VII set.
facts.sourceAgency: South Dakota Legislative Research Council (South Dakota Codified Laws)
facts.notes: Confirmed directly against the primary statute text: SDCL 20-13-10 ('Unfair or discriminatory practices') lists race, color, creed, religion, sex, ancestry, disability, and national origin verbatim. 'Creed' and 'ancestry' are the additions relative to the federal Title VII set (race, color, religion, sex, national origin).

facts.value: not covered by state law; only federal ADEA applies
facts.summary: Unlike federal law, South Dakota's human rights law does not prohibit age discrimination; age is covered only under the federal ADEA.
facts.sourceAgency: South Dakota Legislative Research Council (South Dakota Codified Laws)
facts.notes: Confirmed by the absence of 'age' from the protected-class list in the primary statute text of SDCL 20-13-10 (race, color, creed, religion, sex, ancestry, disability, national origin -- no age); the DLR's own consumer-facing page states this verbatim as well ('South Dakota law does not cover age discrimination, but this is prohibited under federal law').

facts.summary: South Dakota has no dedicated statute of limitations for wage claims; the general 6-year period under SDCL 15-2-13 for actions on a contract, obligation, or liability (including a liability created by statute) applies to unpaid-wage and overtime claims.
facts.citation: SDCL 15-2-13; SDCL 60-11-1 et seq. (South Dakota Minimum Wage law, no dedicated limitations period)
facts.sourceAgency: South Dakota Legislative Research Council (South Dakota Codified Laws)
facts.notes: SDCL Title 60 sets no dedicated statute of limitations for a wage or overtime claim; SDCL 15-2-13 provides a general 6-year period for 'an action upon a contract, obligation or liability, express or implied' and for 'a liability created by statute,' which is the period ordinarily applied to South Dakota wage claims.

facts.summary: A discrimination charge must be received (notarized) by the South Dakota Division of Human Rights within 180 days of the last alleged discriminatory or unfair practice, or the Division cannot proceed with the case; a charge that is also dual-filed with the EEOC has a separate 300-day federal deadline.
facts.sourceAgency: South Dakota Division of Human Rights, Dept of Labor & Regulation
facts.notes: Confirmed both against DLR's own 'Making a Discrimination Charge' guide (fetched directly) and the primary statute text of SDCL 20-13-31 ('Time for filing charge'), fetched directly from sdlegislature.gov. Shorter than the federal EEOC 300-day deadline available in SD as a deferral state (age-discrimination claims, which SD law does not cover, go to the EEOC only and use the 180-day federal deadline instead, per the DLR guide).

facts.summary: South Dakota law makes it an unfair or discriminatory practice to engage in or threaten any reprisal against a person for filing a discrimination charge, testifying, or assisting in a Human Relations Act proceeding.
facts.sourceAgency: South Dakota Legislative Research Council (South Dakota Codified Laws)
facts.notes: Confirmed directly from the primary statute text. This is South Dakota's anti-retaliation provision tied specifically to discrimination-charge activity under SDCL ch. 20-13; South Dakota has no general private-sector whistleblower statute covering reports of employer wrongdoing generally (narrower, subject-specific statutes exist, e.g. SDCL 34-23A-11 for abortion-referral refusal and SDCL 27B-8-43 for reporting abuse/neglect of a disabled person, neither independently verified this session). South Dakota courts also recognize a common-law public-policy wrongful-discharge claim in limited circumstances, not codified here.
